病历：
The patient was evaluated for suspected primary hyperoxaluria on clinical and biochemical grounds. Kidney function was preserved, with an estimated GFR of 72 mL/min/1.73 m². Two separate 24-hour urine collections demonstrated hyperoxaluria, with oxalate excretion of 75 mg/day and 78 mg/day (upper reference limit 40 mg/day). Enteric and other secondary causes were excluded, with no evidence of fat malabsorption or an enteric source to explain the elevated oxalate.

Genetic testing was performed and confirmed primary hyperoxaluria type 1 (PH1). Pyridoxine responsiveness was then assessed with repeat urinary oxalate measurements after more than 2 weeks of pyridoxine; oxalate decreased from a mean of 76.5 mg/day pre-treatment to a mean of 52 mg/day on pyridoxine, representing a reduction of approximately 32%, but urinary oxalate did not normalize and remained above the upper reference limit. Urinary oxalate excretion remained markedly elevated at 1.9 times the upper reference limit. There were no features of an active clinical phenotype, with no ongoing stone disease, nephrocalcinosis, or renal impairment documented, and it was also not the case that there was no ongoing clinical disease.

Primary clinical focus: management.
